questions.prompt: An owner says lots of new faces try her studio, but her member count barely moves. Where do you focus?

options.text: The path from intro offer to membership
The look of her studio's Instagram feed
The number of classes on her schedule
The brand of mats she sells at the desk

questions.reveal: New faces only pay off when they become members. Ask what happens after the intro offer, then show the intro-to-member path.

questions.prompt: According to the training's research, how are most yoga teachers paid?

options.text: A salary that includes health benefits
Per class, per head, or a mix of both
A share of the studio's yearly sales
An hourly rate for front-desk shifts

questions.reveal: Per-class flat rates are most common, with per-head pay or a base plus a per-head bonus. Most teachers are contractors.

questions.prompt: An owner's evening classes are full, but her midday classes run a third full. Why does that matter to her?

options.text: Small classes count against her license
Small classes can't be booked online
Rent and most pay are owed at any size
Midday clients only buy single drop-ins

questions.reveal: Rent and most teacher pay don't shrink with the class, so how full classes are drives her profit.

questions.prompt: What does the training say about when new yoga students decide whether to stay?

options.text: Only after their first full year there
Each time their class pack runs out
Only when the studio raises its prices
Mostly within their first 4 to 6 weeks

questions.reveal: Jonathan Fields writes that most new students decide in their first four to six weeks, so the intro-to-member path matters most.

questions.prompt: What does ClassPass's 2025 Look Back Report say about yoga?

options.text: Bookings fell for the third year
Second most-booked, behind Pilates
Most-booked workout for 3 years
Only hot yoga grew in bookings

questions.reveal: Yoga was the second most-booked workout. Pilates was first for the third year, and both grew.

questions.prompt: Yoga Alliance's study found the top reason Americans start yoga is now:

options.text: Stress release
Flexibility
Weight loss
Injury rehab

questions.reveal: Stress release is now the top reason. In 2016 it was flexibility.

questions.prompt: A hot yoga owner says her front desk forgets to ask first-timers if they've done hot yoga before. What do you show?

options.text: A reminder note taped to the desk
A survey emailed after the class
A tag the teacher adds after class
Custom questions asked at checkout

questions.reveal: The studio writes its own checkout questions, so every new student answers before class and the answers reach the roster.

questions.prompt: Her hot room fits 20 students, but aerial has only 11 hammocks. What does she need?

options.text: One capacity number for the studio
A separate account for aerial only
Capacity set on each class template
Spot booking turned off for aerial

questions.reveal: Capacity is set class by class, so aerial can cap at its hammocks while hot classes take more.

questions.prompt: An owner wants brand-new students to see only her intro offer first. What do you show?

options.text: A promo code she posts on her Instagram
A pop-up form that asks for their email
An offer set as buyable first membership
A welcome email sent after they book

questions.reveal: An offer can be purchasable only as a first membership and shown first, so a new student sees the easiest way in.

questions.prompt: A new client buys a class pack from a class's page. What happens?

options.text: She's also enrolled in that class
She has to go back and book again
She's added to that class's waitlist
The studio has to enroll her by hand

questions.reveal: Buying a pack from a class page enrolls her in that class, so nobody buys credits and then shows up off the roster.

questions.prompt: A switching owner worries that migrated clients will buy her intro offer a second time. What fits?

options.text: Take the intro offer off her website
Ask clients not to buy it a second time
Charge the full price to everyone now
Tag past clients and restrict the intro

questions.reveal: Tag past clients during migration and limit the intro to everyone else. Onboarding sets up the details.

questions.prompt: An owner wants an automatic voicemail to every new intro student. Momence doesn't place automatic calls. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's coming in the next release
Say so, then offer a staff call task
Say yes and let onboarding sort it out
Skip the question and show sequences

questions.reveal: Say it plainly, then offer what works: a recorded message in an email or text, or a sequence step that creates a staff task to call.

questions.prompt: Per the ClassPass partner guide, why do studios run teacher trainings?

options.text: It's required to keep the studio open
It replaces their weekly class revenue
Students can't practice without one
Extra income, new teachers, community

questions.reveal: Trainings use empty studio time, add income, help find new teachers and build community. Many trainees join to deepen their own practice.

questions.prompt: An owner says workshops and retreats get lost in her busy class schedule. What fits?

options.text: Fewer classes on her weekly schedule
A text blast before each workshop
A separate calendar just for events
Listing events only in her newsletter

questions.reveal: Events and workshops can sit on their own calendar on her site, apart from the class schedule, or on one calendar if she prefers.

questions.prompt: An owner wants to fill a workshop with her most regular students. What do you show?

options.text: A segment by visits, then the event link
A ClassPass listing for the workshop
A flyer posted at the front desk
An ad aimed at people who never came

questions.reveal: Segment clients by recent visits and send them the workshop's own link by email, text or in-app.

questions.prompt: An owner wants her five-class rolling pass to work for sound baths too. What do you show?

options.text: A separate pass just for events
Choosing what the pack includes
A promo code for sound baths only
A price rule on a sound-bath tag

questions.reveal: Each pack lists exactly which classes and events it covers, so the owner can add sound baths to it.

questions.prompt: A prospect says she felt “on her own” after her last system's onboarding. What should your demo make sure to cover?

options.text: How many reports come built in
How help works once she's live
How the branded app is approved
How to design her gift cards

questions.reveal: Support after onboarding is the pain she named, so show how she gets help once she's live. Quote only what you can confirm.

questions.prompt: Which frustrations do vendor buyer guides and our yoga demos both point to?

options.text: Too many class styles on the schedule
Waivers that clients have to sign
Booking pages that load too quickly
Add-on fees and support hard to reach

questions.reveal: Surprise fees, slow support and onboarding that leaves owners on their own come up in research and in our calls.

questions.prompt: An owner says her older, small-town clients would mind paying card fees. What do you do?

options.text: Accept it and move on without pushing
Explain the fee pass-through again
Say every studio passes fees on now
Insist it's the only way to save

questions.reveal: Passing fees on is her choice. Pushing after she says no cost the AE trust in our Pure Yoga demo.

questions.prompt: A brand-new owner asks where new students will come from. What did our demos point to?

options.text: The Momence app's list of nearby studios
Free ads Momence runs for new studios
ClassPass, Google reviews and referrals
A partner network Momence sends leads to

questions.reveal: Momence isn't a marketplace. New studios got students from ClassPass, Google reviews and referrals, then booked them on their own site.
